A conductor is said to have reached electrostatic equilibrium when its charge distribution becomes stable.

[[File:Electrostatic-induction.svg|500px|center]]

For example, all conductors in the picture above have reached electrostatic equilibrium.

== Properties ==

Consider a solid conductor $(S)$ at electrostatic equilibrium.

By combination of [[Classical_mechanics#Newton's_2nd_law|Newton's 2nd law]] and [[Electric_charge#Electrostatic_force|Coulomb's law]], for any macroscopic charge $A$:

$$\vec a = \frac{Q_A\vec E}{m}$$

By definition of electrostatic equilibrium, 

$$
\forall A \in (S), \vec a=0 \\
\therefore \vec E =0 \text{ for every point inside (S)  (1)}
$$

As a result, if conductor $(S)$ is charged, any charge must be destributed on the surface of $(S)$, $S(S)$, which creates an electric field on $S(S)$. 

This field must satisfy $\vec E \bot S(S)$ at all points. (3) Otherwise, the macroscopic charges would move along the surface.

=== Summary ===

To summarise, the three properties for a conductor at electrostatic equilibrium are:

# $\vec E_{internal}=0$
# charges may exist only on the surface of the conductor
# on the surface, $\vec E =0 \lor \vec E \bot \text {surface}$
